newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Hashimoto backs Seoul's demands for North apology.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto backs Seoul's demands for North apology.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Sunday he supported South Korean demands for the North to apologise to Seoul over a submarine incident last September, a Japanese Foreign Ministry official said.

Hashimoto also offered South Korean President Kim Young-sam condolences for South Korean victims killed in shootouts with the armed crew of the North Korean submarine, which went aground off the South, the senior Japanese official said.
The ministry official discussed issues raised at the Kim-Hashimoto talks, held in Manila on the eve of Monday's summit meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.
"We understand South Korea's position on the submarine incident, and agree that North Korea should take steps that would convince you," the official quoted Hashimoto as telling Kim.

The crew of the North Korean submarine landed in South territory and triggered a widespread hunt by South Korean troops. One of the North Koreans was captured and 24 of the remaining 25 were killed. One crew member is still missing.
North Korea demanded the return of the vessel, the captured crew and the bodies of the dead crew, but the South demanded an apology and a promise that such incidents would not occur again.

At Sunday's meeting, Kim restated his demand for an apology from Pyongyang, although he did say there was no fundamental change in calls for four-party peace talks with the North that would also include China and the United States.
There was also no change in South Korea's participation in a U.S.-led consortium -- called Korean Energy Development Organisation (KEDO) -- to replace the North's plutonium-breeding nuclear reactors.

"There is no change on our position over KEDO and the four-party talks, but North Korea should issue an apology about such military provocations and promise such incidents would not occur again," the Japanese official quoted Kim was as telling Hashimoto.
North Korea recently threatened to pull out of the 1994 KEDO deal, blaming South Korea for escalating the submarine row.

Kim accepted an invitation from Hashimoto to visit Japan early next year and the two leaders agreed to hold informal talks based on a meeting held on the South Korean island of Cheju in June, the official said. No date was set.
Hashimoto and Kim spent a considerable time discussing bilateral cooperation in international organisations, the official said.
"Japan-South Korea ties were restricted mostly to bilateral issues but now this is changing," Hashimoto told Kim.
In January, Japan joins South Korea as a non-permanent member of the U.N. Security Council and the two leaders agreed to step up joint efforts in various forums.

These include APEC, future meetings of the Asia-Europe ASEM conference, the World Trade Organisation, the Paris-based Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and the Security Council, the Japanese official said.
Kim and Hashimoto agreed to speed up bilateral negotiations over the U.N. Law of the Sea, which both countries ratified this year, the official said.
But the two did not discuss a thorny dispute over a group of small islands in the Sea of Japan, called Takeshima by Japan and Tokdo by South Korea, the official said.
Public outrage at Japan flared up in South Korea this year after Japanese government officials made public statements about Tokyo's claims to the islands. The islands are held by South Korea.
The two leaders also did not take up the question of Japanese Emperor Akihito's trip to South Korea for the opening ceremony of the 2002 Korea-Japan Soccer World Cup, the official said.
Anti-emperor sentiment in South Korea still runs high, a legacy of Japan's brutal colonisation of the Korean Peninsula up to 1945.
